title: Web Push, WhatsApp, and notifications
summary: Manage permissions, Service Workers, webhooks, and preferences to send the right message through the right channel without spam.

lessons.title: Web Push subscription with consent
prerequisites: Understand browser permissions, Service Workers, signed webhooks, and the difference between consent and channel preference.
Be able to restate “VAPID” before coding: A key pair identifying the application server to the Push service without authenticating the user.
Know how to create exercises/23-notifications/push-subscription.ts, run npm run build, and compare real output with a written expectation.
objectives: Request permission after user intent, create the subscription with the public VAPID key, and make unsubscribe as easy as subscribe.

Build a subscription flow that respects denial and does not confuse permission with server registration, then prove the result with this exact signal: a refusal leaves the UI functional without prompting again; consent creates a subscription tied to user, browser, and revocation date.

blocks.text: A notification is a decision before it is a message: eligible event, authorized recipient, available channel, acceptable frequency, then observable delivery. In “Web Push subscription with consent”, the concrete input is an explicit button lets the user request Push, then sends the subscription to the server only after granted. VAPID means: A key pair identifying the application server to the Push service without authenticating the user. The model is complete only when you explain value and frequency, wait for a gesture, treat default and denied as choices, and provide server-side unsubscribe and can observe that a refusal leaves the UI functional without prompting again; consent creates a subscription tied to user, browser, and revocation date.

blocks.title: Simple analogy
blocks.text: A notification orchestrator is a switchboard: it chooses an authorized line and avoids calling three times with the same information. Here the part you will actually inspect is a subscription flow that respects denial and does not confuse permission with server registration; stop using the analogy if it obscures the technical boundary shown by the code.

Start by bounding this lesson’s case: an explicit button lets the user request Push, then sends the subscription to the server only after granted. Request permission after user intent, create the subscription with the public VAPID key, and make unsubscribe as easy as subscribe. The term VAPID is not a decorative label: A key pair identifying the application server to the Push service without authenticating the user. It determines what enters, which authority may act, and which observation counts as evidence rather than an impression.

In exercises/23-notifications/push-subscription.ts, the example deliberately reduces the system to a subscription flow that respects denial and does not confuse permission with server registration. Read each line as one responsibility, then run npm run build. The main failure to trigger is: requestPermission runs on page load without gesture or explanation, pushing the user toward a lasting refusal. It shows why the professional correction is to explain value and frequency, wait for a gesture, treat default and denied as choices, and provide server-side unsubscribe, not to conceal the error.

In a real system, the happy path is only one case among retries, invalid input, and partial outages. The expected proof is that a refusal leaves the UI functional without prompting again; consent creates a subscription tied to user, browser, and revocation date. Apply the same evidence to order alerts, product availability, and WhatsApp support conversations, using a correlation trace without secrets or personal data so both success and failure remain explainable.
